# Fully Flexible Probabilities

<!-- badges: start -->
[![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental)
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/Reckziegel/FFP/workflows/R-CMD-check/badge.svg)](https://github.com/Reckziegel/FFP/actions)
[![Codecov test coverage](https://codecov.io/gh/Reckziegel/FFP/branch/main/graph/badge.svg)](https://app.codecov.io/gh/Reckziegel/FFP?branch=main)
[![CRAN status](https://www.r-pkg.org/badges/version/ffp)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=ffp)
[![CRAN RStudio mirror downloads](https://cranlogs.r-pkg.org/badges/last-month/ffp?color=blue)](https://r-pkg.org/pkg/ffp)
[![CRAN RStudio mirror downloads](https://cranlogs.r-pkg.org/badges/grand-total/ffp?color=blue)](https://r-pkg.org/pkg/ffp)
<!-- badges: end -->

Empirical distributions are often built from historical scenarios
that receive equal probability. This is a natural starting point when there is
no reason to consider some scenarios more plausible than others.

In practice, an expert may have an additional information. Fully Flexible Probabilities 
provide a way to incorporate this information without touching in the scenarios. 
Only probabilities are allowed to change.

`ffp` organizes this process into a model workflow. You define the scenario
support, choose prior probabilities, express views about the distribution, and
use Entropy Pooling to obtain posterior probabilities that satisfy those views
while remaining as close as possible to the prior.

## Installation

Install the released version from CRAN with:

```{r eval=FALSE}
install.packages("ffp")
```

You can install the development version from GitHub with:

```{r eval=FALSE}
# install.packages("pak")
devtools::install_github("Reckziegel/FFP")
```

## A model-first workflow

Consider 500 simulated scenarios for equity returns, bond returns, and
inflation:

```{r}
library(ffp)

set.seed(123)

scenarios <- tibble::tibble(
  equity    = rnorm(500, mean = 0.006, sd = 0.04),
  bonds     = rnorm(500, mean = 0.002, sd = 0.012),
  inflation = rnorm(500, mean = 0.025, sd = 0.007)
)
scenarios
```

Each row represents one possible scenario. At this point, the data describe
what can happen, but we have not yet specified how probable each scenario
should be.

#### Define the scenario support

The first step is to create an `ffp` model from the scenarios:

```{r}
model <- ffp_model(scenarios)
model
```

`ffp_model()` defines the support of the empirical distribution. These
scenarios remain fixed throughout the Entropy Pooling workflow.

#### Choose a prior

Next, we specify the probabilities we want to assign before incorporating any
views.

A uniform prior gives every scenario the same initial probability:

```{r}
model <- model |>
  ffp_prior(
    prior_uniform()
  )
model
```

The prior represents what we believe about the scenarios before introducing
additional information.

#### Add a view

Suppose we believe that the expected equity return should be 1%. We express this directly as a view on the model:

```{r}
model <- model |>
  ffp_view(
    view_mean(equity, target = 0.01)
  )
model
```

A view describes a property that we want the posterior distribution to satisfy.
Here, it concerns the posterior mean of `equity`.

#### Fit the model

Finally, we combine the prior and the view using Entropy Pooling:

```{r}
fit <- ffp_fit(model)
fit
```

`ffp_fit()` finds posterior scenario probabilities that satisfy the view while
remaining as close as possible to the prior in relative-entropy terms. The
scenario support remains unchanged; only the probabilities are updated.

Once the individual steps are familiar, the same model can be written as a
single pipeline:

```{r eval=FALSE}
fit <- scenarios |>
  ffp_model() |>
  ffp_prior(
    prior_uniform()
  ) |>
  ffp_view(
    view_mean(equity, target = 0.01)
  ) |>
  ffp_fit()
```

## Understanding the posterior

Because the fitted model retains the scenarios, the prior and
posterior probabilities, distributional changes can be inspected directly:

```{r}
stats <- ffp_stats(fit)
stats
```

To understand what happened to a particular variable:

```{r}
summary(stats, variable = "equity")
```

Tail risk can be inspected using the usual loss convention:

```{r}
ffp_risk(fit, confidence = 0.99)
```

The same posterior probabilities can therefore be used to study changes in
location, dispersion, shape, tail risk, and the effective number of scenarios.

## Priors and views

A uniform prior is only the simplest starting point.

`ffp` can construct priors from time decay (`prior_exp_decay()`), rolling windows (`prior_rolling_window()`), 
market conditioning (`prior_crisp()`), custom probabilities (`prior_custom()`), or 
combinations of different prior specifications (`prior_product()` and `prior_mixture()`).

```{r eval=FALSE}
prior_exp_decay(half_life = 60)
prior_kernel(inflation, target = 0.03, bandwidth = 0.005)
```

Views can describe different features of the posterior distribution:

```{r eval=FALSE}
view_mean(equity, target = 0.01)
view_probability(inflation > 0.04, target = 0.20)
view_quantile(equity, target = -0.08, level = 0.05)
```

Several views can be attached to the same model and processed jointly.

## Partial confidence

`ffp_fit()` computes the full-confidence Entropy Pooling posterior.

When a view should influence the distribution without being imposed with full
confidence, the prior and full-confidence posterior can subsequently be combined
through opinion pooling:

```{r eval=TRUE}
pooled <- ffp_opinion_pooling(fit, confidence = 0.75)
pooled
```

View confidence is a modeling choice and is distinct from numerical solver
tolerances.

Additional details of the final fit can be inspected with the `summary` helper:

```{r}
summary(pooled)
```

## ffp 2.0

`ffp` 2.0 introduces a higher-level, model-first interface built around
`ffp_model()`, `ffp_prior()`, `ffp_view()`, and `ffp_fit()`.

Lower-level probability, view, and Entropy Pooling functions remain available,
but the model workflow is the recommended starting point for new analyses.
